los.text: Describe the main causes, signs and symptoms and pathophysiology of pyrexia, and explain the principles of diagnosis and treatment
los.html:
FeverCore temperature ≥38 °C due to a raised hypothalamic set point (differs from hyperthermia).
Pathophysiology
  • PAMPs (e.g. LPS)
  • → macrophages release pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α)
  • → hypothalamic endothelium (OVLT)
  • → COX-2 → PGE2
  • → ↑ set point in preoptic area
  • → heat conservation and production.
Causes
  • Infection (most common)
  • Inflammatory/autoimmune (vasculitis, SLE, IBD, Still's)
  • Malignancy (lymphoma, RCC, leukaemia)
  • Drugs (drug fever, NMS, serotonin syndrome)
  • Thrombosis (PE)
  • Endocrine (thyroid storm)
  • Tissue damage (MI, surgery, transfusion reactions).
Pyrexia of unknown origin>38.3 °C on several occasions for >3 weeks without diagnosis despite investigation (infection, malignancy, connective tissue disease).
ApproachHistory (travel, contacts, sexual, IVDU, animals, drugs, immunosuppression, localising symptoms), full exam (rashes, murmurs, lymphadenopathy, joints, lines, wounds), sepsis screen (NEWS2, lactate).
Ix
  • FBC (neutrophilia, lymphopenia), CRP/procalcitonin, U&E, LFT, blood cultures before antibiotics, urine dipstick/culture, CXR, targeted samples (sputum, CSF, swabs)
  • Malaria films if travel
  • Echo (endocarditis)
  • Imaging/PET-CT for PUO.
Treatment
  • Treat cause
  • Antipyretics (paracetamol, NSAIDs: comfort, don't prevent febrile convulsions), fluids
  • Empirical antibiotics urgently if sepsis or neutropenia (within 1 h)
  • Otherwise targeted therapy.

los.text: Explain the factors that influence patient expectations of antibiotic prescription and the public health needs to reduce prescription (eg. Antibiotic resistance)
los.html:
Patient expectations
  • Belief antibiotics cure colds/coughs (most respiratory tract infections are viral and self-limiting)
  • Previous experience of "getting better on antibiotics"
  • Wanting a tangible outcome/validation
  • Time off work
  • Fear of serious illness (parents of young children)
  • Cultural norms
  • Internet/media
  • Lack of knowledge of resistance and side effects.
Prescriber factorsPerceived patient expectation (often overestimated), time pressure, diagnostic uncertainty, fear of complications/litigation, wish to maintain relationship, out-of-hours settings.
Public health need
  • Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is driven by overuse and misuse
  • Projected to cause ~10 million deaths/year globally by 2050 if unchecked.
  • Also side effects, C. difficile, cost, microbiome disruption.
Strategies
  • Consultation: explore ICE; explain natural history (e.g. cough 3 weeks, sore throat 1 week); safety-net advice; delayed (back-up) prescribing; self-care advice; TARGET leaflets; FeverPAIN/Centor scores for sore throat; CRP point-of-care testing.
  • Systems: UK National Action Plan for AMR, stewardship programmes, audit and feedback, prescribing targets, public campaigns ("Keep Antibiotics Working"), One Health (agriculture).

los.text: Describe the stages of fever and explain the signs and symptoms that accompany these stages
los.html:
StageMechanismSigns/symptoms
1. Onset (chill phase)Set point ↑ but body temp still "too low" → heat conservation and productionFeels cold, shivering/rigors, pale, cool peripheries (vasoconstriction), piloerection, seeks warmth, temperature rises
2. Plateau (fever/stable)Body temp reaches new set point
  • Hot, flushed, dry skin, malaise, tachycardia (~10 bpm per °C), tachypnoea, thirst, headache, myalgia, anorexia, delirium in elderly
  • Febrile convulsions in young children
3. Defervescence (flush/resolution)Set point returns to normal (cause resolves or antipyretic) → heat lossSweating, flushed warm skin (vasodilation), feels hot, temperature falls; risk of dehydration
PatternsContinuous, intermittent (spikes returning to normal: abscess, malaria), remittent, relapsing (Pel–Ebstein in Hodgkin's), tertian/quartan (malaria).
Benefits of feverInhibits microbial growth, enhances immune function. Treat for comfort, not to prevent febrile seizures.

los.text: Describe drug-drug and drug-food interactions and the potential clinical implications and management strategies for such interactions
los.html:
Pharmacokinetic interactions
  • Absorption: chelation (tetracyclines/quinolones + calcium, iron, antacids, dairy → separate by 2 h); ↑ gastric pH reduces ketoconazole absorption; levothyroxine with calcium/iron.
  • Distribution: protein-binding displacement (usually minor).
  • Metabolism: CYP450 inhibitors ↑ levels ("SICKFACES.COM": Sodium valproate, Isoniazid, Cimetidine, Ketoconazole/azoles, Fluconazole, Alcohol (acute), Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin/clarithromycin, Sulfonamides, Ciprofloxacin, Omeprazole, Metronidazole) and grapefruit juice (CYP3A4: ↑ simvastatin, CCBs, ciclosporin). CYP450 inducers ↓ levels ("PC BRAS": Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Barbiturates, Rifampicin, Alcohol (chronic), Sulfonylureas) and St John's wort (↓ OCP, warfarin, ciclosporin).
  • Excretion: ↓ lithium clearance with NSAIDs/ACEi/thiazides; methotrexate + trimethoprim/NSAIDs.
Pharmacodynamic interactionsAdditive (NSAID + warfarin → bleeding; QT-prolonging drugs; serotonergic drugs → serotonin syndrome; CNS depressants; ACEi + spironolactone → ↑K⁺) or antagonistic (β-blocker + salbutamol).
Drug–foodWarfarin + vitamin K-rich greens/cranberry, MAOIs + tyramine (cheese, cured meats → hypertensive crisis), alcohol + metronidazole (disulfiram-like), grapefruit, dairy with antibiotics.
High-risk drugsNarrow therapeutic index (warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, ciclosporin, theophylline).
ManagementCheck BNF Appendix 1, avoid combination, adjust dose, separate administration timing, monitor levels/INR/U&E, counsel patients.

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology, presentation and principles of treatment of hyperthermia (heat exhaustion and heat stroke)
los.html:
Hyperthermia↑ core temperature with a normal set point because heat gain exceeds heat loss (so antipyretics don't work).
Causes
  • Environmental heat/humidity
  • Exertion
  • Impaired heat loss (elderly, infants, obesity, dehydration, heavy clothing)
  • Drugs (anticholinergics ↓ sweating, diuretics, MDMA/cocaine/amphetamines)
  • Malignant hyperthermia
  • NMS
  • Serotonin syndrome
  • Thyroid storm.
Heat exhaustionHeat stroke
Core tempUsually <40 °C>40 °C
CNSNormal mental stateCNS dysfunction: confusion, ataxia, seizures, coma
FeaturesFatigue, headache, nausea, dizziness, heavy sweating, tachycardia, cramps, syncopeHot skin (may be dry in classic, sweating in exertional), multi-organ failure: rhabdomyolysis, AKI, liver failure, DIC
RxMove to cool place, rest, oral/IV fluids, coolMedical emergency: ABCDE, rapid cooling (cold water immersion for exertional; evaporative cooling, ice packs to groin/axillae), IV fluids, treat complications
  • Classic (elderly, heatwaves, gradual) vs exertional (young athletes, soldiers, rapid).
  • Malignant hyperthermia: dantrolene. Prevention: hydration, acclimatisation, avoid midday exertion, check vulnerable people in heatwaves.

los.text: Identify organelles and structures within the cell membranes and link them to function and likely pathology
los.html:
Plasma membrane
  • Phospholipid bilayer (fluid mosaic) + cholesterol + proteins (channels, carriers, pumps, receptors, adhesion molecules) + glycocalyx.
  • Functions: barrier, transport, signalling, adhesion.
  • Pathology: channelopathies (CFTR in cystic fibrosis), receptor defects (LDL receptor in FH, insulin resistance), membrane damage by toxins (pore-forming toxins, complement MAC), lipid peroxidation in injury.
Membrane-bound organelles(also see next LO)
  • Mitochondria (double membrane; ATP; apoptosis → mitochondrial disorders)
  • ER
  • Golgi
  • Lysosomes (single membrane, acid hydrolases → lysosomal storage diseases: Gaucher, Tay–Sachs)
  • Peroxisomes (very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation → Zellweger, adrenoleukodystrophy)
  • Nucleus (nuclear envelope with pores).
SpecialisationFunctionLinked pathology
MicrovilliAbsorptionLost in coeliac disease
Cilia (9+2 microtubules)MovementPrimary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener's: bronchiectasis, infertility, situs inversus
Tight junctionsBarrier
Desmosomes/adherensAdhesionPemphigus (anti-desmoglein)
Gap junctionsCommunication
HemidesmosomesAnchor to basement membraneBullous pemphigoid
  • Reversible cell injury shows membrane blebbing and swelling (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase failure); irreversible injury = membrane rupture.

los.text: List the 7 main groups of infectious organisms and outline how they can be classified based on cell structure and size
los.html:
GroupSizeStructureExamples
PrionsProtein onlyMisfolded PrPˢᶜ; no nucleic acidCJD, vCJD
Viruses20–300 nmNucleic acid (DNA or RNA) + capsid ± envelope; obligate intracellularInfluenza, HIV, herpes
Bacteria0.5–5 μmProkaryotic (no nucleus, 70S ribosomes), cell wall (Gram +/−, acid-fast)Staph, E. coli, TB
FungiYeasts 3–10 μm; moulds (hyphae)Eukaryotic, chitin cell wall, ergosterol membraneCandida, Aspergillus, dermatophytes
Protozoa10–100 μmSingle-celled eukaryotes, no cell wallPlasmodium, Giardia, Entamoeba, Toxoplasma
Helminths (metazoa)mm to metresMulticellular worms: nematodes (round), cestodes (tape), trematodes (flukes)Ascaris, Taenia, Schistosoma
Ectoparasites (arthropods)mmMulticellularScabies mite, lice
Bacterial classification
  • Gram stain (positive: thick peptidoglycan; negative: thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane with LPS)
  • Shape (cocci, bacilli, spirochaetes)
  • Arrangement (clusters, chains)
  • Oxygen requirements (aerobe, anaerobe)
  • Biochemical tests
  • Molecular methods (16S rRNA, MALDI-TOF).
Size mattersFilters, microscopy needed (electron microscopy for viruses), route of spread (airborne droplet nuclei).

los.text: Outline the mechanisms by which pathogens cause damage to host cells and tissues
los.html:
Direct damage
  • Exotoxins: cytotoxins (diphtheria toxin stops protein synthesis; Shiga toxin), pore-forming toxins (S. aureus α-toxin, streptolysin), enterotoxins (cholera → secretion), neurotoxins (tetanus, botulinum), superantigens (TSST-1: massive T-cell activation → cytokine storm).
  • Enzymes: collagenase, hyaluronidase, proteases, phospholipases (C. perfringens α-toxin → gas gangrene).
  • Intracellular replication → cell lysis (viruses, Shigella, Plasmodium in RBCs).
  • Endotoxin (LPS) → systemic inflammation, septic shock, DIC.
Indirect (immune-mediated) damage
  • Excessive inflammation (abscess, granulomas: TB caseation)
  • Cytotoxic T cells killing infected cells (hepatitis B)
  • Immune complexes (post-strep glomerulonephritis)
  • Molecular mimicry (rheumatic fever, Guillain–Barré).
OtherObstruction (worms, biofilm on devices), oncogenesis (HPV, EBV, HBV, H. pylori), nutrient competition (tapeworms → B12), altered cell function (viral latency).

los.text: List the strategies pathogens use to evade the host immune system
los.html:
Avoid recognitionAntigenic variation (influenza drift/shift, HIV, Trypanosoma VSG, Neisseria pili), latency (herpesviruses hide in neurons), intracellular niches (TB inside macrophages, Plasmodium in RBCs/liver).
Resist phagocytosisCapsules (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib), M protein (S. pyogenes), protein A (S. aureus: binds IgG Fc), leukocidins (PVL kills neutrophils).
Survive inside phagocytesInhibit phagolysosome fusion (M. tuberculosis), escape into cytoplasm (Listeria), resist oxidative killing (catalase, SOD).
Inactivate antibodies/complementIgA protease (Neisseria, Haemophilus, pneumococcus), complement inhibitors, sialic acid coats.
Interfere with antigen presentation/T cellsViral downregulation of MHC class I (CMV, HIV), HIV kills CD4 cells, superantigens cause anergy.
Block interferon responses (many viruses).
BiofilmsProtect from antibodies, phagocytes and antibiotics (prosthetic devices, CF Pseudomonas).
Molecular mimicry of host molecules.

los.html:

ViralNorovirus (outbreaks, vomiting, 1–3 days), rotavirus (children; vaccine), adenovirus 40/41, hepatitis A/ESelf-limiting watery diarrhoea
Bacterial

  • C. difficile (antibiotics, PPIs; pseudomembranous colitis)
  • S. aureus/B. cereus toxins (rapid vomiting; reheated rice)
  • Listeria (pregnancy)
  • H. pylori (stomach)
FungalCandida (oral/oesophageal thrush in immunosuppressed), HistoplasmaRare in immunocompetent
ProtozoalGiardia (bloating, steatorrhoea; metronidazole), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery, flask-shaped ulcers, liver abscess), Cryptosporidium (water; severe in HIV), CyclosporaStool microscopy/PCR

  • Taenia (tapeworm; T. solium → cysticercosis)

Eosinophilia

los.text: Describe common viral, bacterial and fungal infections of the skin
los.html:
GroupOrganisms / conditionsFeatures
Viral
  • HSV-1/2 (cold sores, genital herpes; grouped vesicles)
  • VZV (chickenpox, shingles)
  • HPV (warts, verrucae)
  • Molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus: umbilicated papules)
  • Hand
  • Foot and mouth (coxsackie)
  • Measles/rubella (exanthems)
  • Parvovirus B19 ("slapped cheek")
Vesicles, papules, exanthems
Bacterial
  • S. aureus: impetigo (honey-crusted), folliculitis, boils/carbuncles, abscess, SSSS (children), PVL strains.
  • S. pyogenes: cellulitis, erysipelas (sharp raised margin), impetigo, necrotising fasciitis (also polymicrobial), scarlet fever.
  • Others: erythrasma (Corynebacterium), Lyme disease (erythema migrans), leprosy
Rx: flucloxacillin (clarithromycin if allergic); topical fusidic acid/hydrogen peroxide for localised impetigo
Fungal
  • Dermatophytes (Trichophyton): tinea pedis, corporis (ring with central clearing), cruris, capitis, unguium (onychomycosis)
  • Candida: intertrigo, nappy rash (satellite lesions), paronychia
  • Malassezia: pityriasis versicolor, seborrhoeic dermatitis
Diagnose with skin scrapings (KOH microscopy, culture). Rx: topical azoles/terbinafine; oral terbinafine for nails
  • Ectoparasites: scabies (burrows in finger webs, intense nocturnal itch; permethrin to whole household), head lice.
